name: Usher syndrome
aliases: retinitis pigmentosa with sensorineural hearing loss

clinicalPearls: The defining combination is congenital sensorineural hearing loss together with progressive retinitis pigmentosa, producing dual sensory (deaf-blind) impairment
Inheritance is autosomal recessive, with many causative genes encoding proteins of the hair-cell and photoreceptor cilium (the 'Usher interactome'), including MYO7A, USH2A and CDH23
Type 1 features profound congenital deafness with absent vestibular function and delayed motor milestones from balance impairment
Type 2 features moderate-to-severe hearing loss with preserved vestibular function, and is the commonest subtype
Type 3 is characterised by progressive, later-onset hearing loss and variable vestibular findings
Night blindness and constricting peripheral (tunnel) vision from retinitis pigmentosa often appear later than the hearing loss, so early audiology cases may be missed as isolated deafness
Suspect Usher in any child with congenital sensorineural hearing loss, and arrange ophthalmology and electroretinography follow-up to detect retinal disease early
reference.pathophysiology: Usher syndrome is a group of autosomal recessive disorders caused by mutations in genes whose protein products are needed for the structure and function of stereocilia in cochlear hair cells and of the connecting cilium in retinal photoreceptors. Loss of these shared proteins impairs mechanotransduction in the inner ear and progressive degeneration of rod and cone photoreceptors, giving the characteristic combination of sensorineural hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa. In some subtypes vestibular hair cells are also affected, producing balance disturbance. The clinical subtype reflects which gene is involved and the severity of the resulting protein defect.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital rubella and other congenital infections affecting eye and ear
Alstrom syndrome and other ciliopathies with sensory loss
Refsum disease with retinopathy and neuropathy
Bardet-Biedl syndrome and mitochondrial disease with combined sensory involvement
additionalInvestigations: Pure-tone and paediatric audiometry with otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response
Vestibular function testing to help distinguish subtypes
Electroretinography to detect early photoreceptor dysfunction before symptomatic visual loss
Dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography for retinitis pigmentosa
Molecular genetic testing (gene panel) to confirm the diagnosis and subtype
redFlags: Congenital deafness with delayed independent walking, suggesting vestibular involvement and type 1 disease
Progressive night blindness or narrowing visual field in a deaf child
Family history of combined hearing and visual loss
Deterioration in mobility and orientation from combined sensory decline
reference.prognosis: Hearing loss is generally stable or slowly progressive depending on subtype, while retinitis pigmentosa is progressive and can lead to severe visual impairment in adulthood; early cochlear implantation and low-vision support substantially improve communication and independence.
pitfalls: Attributing congenital hearing loss to an isolated cause and not screening for retinal disease
Mislabelling early balance and motor delay as global developmental delay rather than vestibular loss
Assuming normal vision excludes Usher, as retinopathy often manifests later
Failing to arrange genetic counselling for an autosomal recessive condition with recurrence risk
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
